{{Short description|Mathematical term in group theory}}
[[File:Prüfer.png|thumb|upright=1.3|class=skin-invert-image|The Prüfer {{math|2}}-group with presentation {{math|{{angbr|1=''g''<sub>''n''</sub>: ''g''<sub>''n''+1</sub><sup>2</sup> = ''g''<sub>''n''</sub>, ''g''<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> = ''e''}}}}, illustrated as a subgroup of the unit circle in the complex plane]]
{{Ring theory sidebar}}

In mathematics, specifically in [[group theory]], the '''Prüfer ''p''-group''' or the '''''p''-quasicyclic group''' or <math>p^\infty</math>-group, <math>\mathbb Z(p^\infty)</math>, for a [[prime number]] ''p'' is the unique [[p-group|''p''-group]] in which every element has ''p'' different ''p''-th roots. 

The Prüfer ''p''-groups are [[countable set|countable]] [[abelian group|abelian groups]] that are important in the classification of infinite abelian groups: they (along with the group of [[rational numbers]]) form the smallest building blocks of all [[Divisible group|divisible groups]].

The groups are named after [[Heinz Prüfer]], a German mathematician of the early 20th century.

==Constructions==
The Prüfer ''p''-group may be identified with the subgroup of the [[circle group]], <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math>, consisting of all ''p''<sup>''n''</sup>-th [[root of unity|roots of unity]] as ''n'' ranges over all non-negative integers:
:<math>\begin{align} \mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)&=\{e^{2\pi i m/p^n} \mid 0 \leq m < p^n,\,n\in \mathbb{Z}^+\} \\ &= \{z\in\mathbb{C} \mid z^{(p^n)}=1 \text{ for some } n\in \mathbb{Z}^+\}.\end{align}</math>
The group operation here is the multiplication of [[Complex number|complex numbers]]. There is a [[Group presentation|presentation]]
:<math>\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty) = \langle\, g_1, g_2, g_3, \ldots \mid g_1^p = 1, g_2^p = g_1, g_3^p = g_2, \dots\,\rangle.</math>
Here, the group operation in <math>\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)</math> is written as multiplication. 

Alternatively and equivalently, the Prüfer ''p''-group may be defined as the [[Sylow subgroup|Sylow ''p''-subgroup]] of the [[quotient group]] <math>\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}</math>, consisting of those elements whose order is a power of ''p'':
:<math>\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty) = \mathbb{Z}[1/p]/\mathbb{Z}</math>
(where <math>\mathbb{Z}[1/p]</math> denotes the group of all rational numbers whose denominator is a power of ''p'', using addition of rational numbers as group operation). 

For each natural number ''n'', consider the [[quotient group]] <math>\mathbb{Z}/p^n \mathbb{Z}</math> and the embedding <math>\mathbb{Z}/p^n \mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/p^{n+1} \mathbb{Z}</math> induced by multiplication by ''p''. The [[direct limit]] of this system is <math>\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)</math>:
:<math>\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty) = \varinjlim \mathbb{Z}/p^n \mathbb{Z} .</math>

If we perform the direct limit in the [[category (mathematics)|category]] of [[topological group]]s, then we need to impose a topology on each of the <math>\mathbb{Z}/p^n \mathbb{Z}</math>, and take the [[final topology]] on <math>\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)</math>. If we wish for <math>\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)</math> to be [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]], we must impose the [[discrete topology]] on each of the <math>\mathbb{Z}/p^n \mathbb{Z}</math>, resulting in <math>\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)</math> to have the discrete topology.

We can also write
:<math>\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)=\mathbb{Q}_p/\mathbb{Z}_p</math>
where <math>\mathbb{Q}_p</math> denotes the additive group of [[p-adic number|''p''-adic numbers]] and <math>\mathbb{Z}_p</math> is the subgroup of ''p''-adic integers.

==Properties==
The complete list of subgroups of the Prüfer ''p''-group  <math>\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)</math> is:
:<math>0 \subsetneq \left({1 \over p}\mathbb{Z}\right)/\mathbb{Z} \subsetneq \left({1 \over p^2}\mathbb{Z}\right)/\mathbb{Z} \subsetneq \left({1 \over p^3}\mathbb{Z}\right)/\mathbb{Z} \subsetneq \cdots \subsetneq \mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)</math>
Here, each <math>\left({1 \over p^n}\mathbb{Z}\right)/\mathbb{Z}</math> is a cyclic subgroup of <math>\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)</math> with ''p''<sup>''n''</sup> elements; it contains precisely those elements of <math>\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)</math> whose [[order (group theory)|order]] divides ''p''<sup>''n''</sup> and corresponds to the set of ''p<sup>n</sup>''-th roots of unity.

The Prüfer ''p''-groups are the only infinite groups whose subgroups are [[totally ordered]] by inclusion. This sequence of inclusions expresses the Prüfer ''p''-group as the [[direct limit]] of its finite subgroups. As there is no [[maximal subgroup]] of a Prüfer ''p''-group, it is its own [[Frattini subgroup]].

Given this list of subgroups, it is clear that the Prüfer ''p''-groups are [[indecomposable module|indecomposable]] (cannot be written as a [[direct sum]] of proper subgroups). More is true: the Prüfer ''p''-groups are [[subdirectly irreducible algebra|subdirectly irreducible]]. An abelian group is subdirectly irreducible if and only if it is isomorphic to a finite cyclic ''p''-group or to a Prüfer group.

The Prüfer ''p''-group is the unique infinite [[p-group|''p''-group]] that is [[locally cyclic group|locally cyclic]] (every finite set of elements generates a cyclic group). As seen above, all proper subgroups of <math>\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)</math> are finite. The Prüfer ''p''-groups are the only infinite abelian groups with this property.{{sfnp|Vil'yams|2001}}

The Prüfer ''p''-groups are [[divisible group|divisible]]. They play an important role in the classification of divisible groups; along with the rational numbers they are the simplest divisible groups. More precisely: an abelian group is divisible if and only if it is the [[direct sum]] of a (possibly infinite) number of copies of <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> and (possibly infinite) numbers of copies of <math>\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)</math> for every prime ''p''. The ([[Cardinal number|cardinal]]) numbers of copies of <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> and <math>\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)</math> that are used in this direct sum determine the divisible group up to isomorphism.{{sfnp|Kaplansky|1965}}

As an abelian group (that is, as a [[module (mathematics)|'''Z'''-module]]), <math>\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)</math> is [[Artinian group|Artinian]] but not [[Noetherian group|Noetherian]].{{sfnp|Jacobson|1989|p=102|loc=ex. 2}} It can thus be used as a counterexample against the idea that every Artinian module is Noetherian (whereas every [[Artinian ring|Artinian ''ring'']] is Noetherian).

The [[endomorphism ring]] of <math>\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)</math> is isomorphic to the ring of [[p-adic integers|''p''-adic integers]] <math>\mathbb{Z}_p</math>.{{sfnp|Vil'yams|2001}}

In the theory of [[locally compact topological group]]s the Prüfer ''p''-group (endowed with the [[discrete topology]]) is the [[Pontryagin dual]] of the compact group of [[p-adic integers|''p''-adic integers]], and the group of ''p''-adic integers is the Pontryagin dual of the Prüfer ''p''-group.{{sfnp|Armacost|Armacost|1972}}

==See also==
* [[p-adic integers|''p''-adic integers]], which can be defined as the [[inverse limit]] of the finite subgroups of the Prüfer ''p''-group.
